newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: Russia, Slovakia to intensify economic ties.
newsitem.headline: Russia, Slovakia to intensify economic ties.

text.p: Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin arrives in Slovakia for a two-day visit on Monday for talks on developing economic ties and bound to touch on Slovakia's bid to join NATO.

Russia opposes the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation's eastward expansion plans. Slovakia has said it wants to join the alliance in the first wave of new members but its chances appear to have waned after repeated U.S. and European Union criticism of the pace of democratic reform.
"Our current line is clear. We are and will remain opposed to the enlargement of NATO," Sergei Zotov, Russian ambassador to Slovakia, told a news conference.
"But we recognise that Slovakia must decide its own political line and we do not wish to force our opinion on her."
A spokeswoman for Slovak Prime Minister Vladimir Meciar confirmed that the NATO bid would be discussed.
Slovakia, which became independent when Czechoslovakia split in 1993, is planning to hold a referendum on whether to join NATO on May 23 and 24.

The opposition claims the questions on membership, but also on stationing nuclear weapons or foreign troops, are purposely phrased to turn voters against membership and give Meciar political cover for when Slovakia's bid is turned down.

"The Russians are aware that Slovakia has little or no chance of NATO membership in the first wave of those invited to apply, so they can afford to be less strict," said one diplomat from a NATO member state.

The leading contenders to join the alliance are the Czech Republic, Hungary and Poland. Slovakia has maintained closer ties with Moscow than has the Czech Republic. But the diplomat said Bratislava still believed its future lay with the West.

"I think the Slovaks realise that even if they do not make the first round of membership they still have to strive for integration in western structures if they want to become a functioning economy and democracy," the diplomat said.
The decision on new members will be made formally at a summit of NATO's 16 leaders in Madrid in July. Russian President Boris Yeltsin said on Sunday he has no plans to attend the summit.

Moscow wants commitments that the new members will not upgrade their military facilities to bring them in line with existing NATO countries, and a pledge the alliance will "never" station nuclear weapons on the territory of new members.
NATO and Russian officials are urgently negotiating a treaty on relations between the two sides which Yeltsin said last week would be signed in Paris on May 27.
Zotov said the visit, Chernomyrdin's second as Russian premier, would be mainly devoted to economic ties.

"During his visit Mr Chernomyrdin will sign some 12 accords covering subjects such as liberalisation of trade, cooperation between our central banks and the setting up of a committee for cooperation in science and technology."
Other subjects on the agenda would include cooperation in arms production and whittling down Russia's $1.8 billion debt to Slovakia, inherited from the former Soviet Union.

Zotov said the agreement on liberalising trade stopped well short of an accord on a free trade area, which Meciar has called for in the past, as a result of EU warnings that such a step could jeopardise Slovakia's future membership of the bloc.

"For that reason we have taken the pragmatic path seeking to create a contractual basis that that would not complicate Slovakia's economic cooperation while enriching our mutual commercial cooperation," Zotov said.
